While weight caching primarily reduces I/O latency and startup time, prefix caching significantly accelerates token generation by allowing the model to reuse previously computed attention states for shared context. The primary practical tradeoff lies in memory management, as prefix caching requires substantial GPU memory proportional to the context length and batch size, which can quickly exhaust available resources and limit concurrent user sessions. Consequently, systems must balance the speed gains of prefix reuse against the risk of memory overflow, often necessitating complex eviction policies to maintain stability under high load.

tasks.prompt: Explain the difference between caching model weights and caching a conversation prefix. Use one paragraph of four sentences and include one practical tradeoff.

timings.content: Caching model weights means storing the trained parameters of a model so the same model can be loaded or reused without reloading from disk or retraining. Caching a conversation prefix means storing the intermediate key-value states produced by the model for earlier tokens in a chat, so later turns can continue generation without recomputing those tokens. The first saves model-loading or parameter-transfer overhead, while the second saves per-request prefill computation and can reduce latency for long chats. A practical tradeoff is that prefix caches consume memory proportional to conversation length and batch size, and they may become stale or invalid if the model, prompt template, or quantization changes.

In modern distributed systems, the key-value cache is arguably the most critical component for achieving low-latency performance and high throughput.
